results.summary: Delete this row: the 2017 West Ridge is still known from one report only, so it cannot be written up, and all of the row's content describes the col route that the Southeast Route page already covers.
results.evidence: Searched for a second record of the 2017 West Ridge ('Bring The Noise'): AAJ publications (only the 1962 'First Ascents in the Southern Pickets' note, which covers the 1961 east-ridge ascent from the Otto-Himmel col at class III, plus the 2004 and 2012 enchainment notes, which reach Ottohorn from the col), Mountain Project's Southern Pickets area (no Ottohorn page at all), the peakbagger Picket Range list, the summitpost Picket Range page (archived), the stephabegg Pickets pages and complete-traverse report (both reach Ottohorn via the col), and the 2018 Southern Pickets Enchainment second-ascent report (climbed Ottohorn from the col in about an hour; the old 3rd-class line is gone to rockfall, and they took the fresh scar at about 5.6 rather than the 2-pitch 5.7 variation). No guidebook listing, AAJ report, second ascent or other blog mentions the West Ridge. Every later reply on the first-ascent thread is by the same author or does not describe the ridge, so the thread is one source. Under the two-source standard the West Ridge cannot be written. The row's current content (Class 3-4 with a 5.7 variation, aspect S, the Crescent Creek approach to the Otto-Himmel col, east-ridge descent) is the col route, which is sibling wa_ottohorn_southeast_route ('Southeast Route', from the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col). Rule 3: every documented climb that can be sourced already has a row, so delete. IMPORTANT if the owner instead keeps the row and applies o06's 22-op rewrite: those ops have two errors, found in the same thread. (1) In a November 2017 follow-up the first-ascent author said he had swapped the names of the two sub-summits. The westernmost tower, climbed first on the route, is Honk; the middle one is Beep. o06's face, overview, beta, pitch_detail sections 1-5 and rappels all name them the wrong way round (e.g. 'double-rope rappel off Beep into the Beep-Honk notch' should be off Honk into the Honk-Beep notch). (2) Another climber posted that he had climbed the westernmost tower (Honk) a few weeks before the 2017 party. So the claim that both sub-summits were never climbed before is false for Honk, and o06's fa value 'first ascent ... of the sub-summits Beep and Honk' is wrong. o06's evidence also cites the 1962 AAJ note as a source, but that note predates the route and does not describe it.

results.resolution: rule 3: rewritten as the North Ridge (the documented line best supported by independent accounts; no sibling row exists on wa_half_moon), with the Kangaroo Pass pin and the fictional 'Class 4 step' and heather-gully pins removed
results.summary: Half Moon has no scramble, so this row becomes the North Ridge (Grade III, 5.7+, seven pitches from the notch north of the peak, rappel descent), which two separate accounts describe and which no other row holds.
results.evidence: No scramble or 'Southwest Slopes' route exists: the peak's route pages say there are at least three difficult routes and no easy one, and the peak's encyclopedia entry puts the easiest route at class 5+. wa_half_moon has only this row, so the documented climbs are South Face (5.9+ or 5.7 A0, III, 5 pitches), North Ridge (5.7+, III, 7 pitches), and the 2017 Uncle Wehrly's Toupee (5.10-, which finishes on Choi Oi Tower, not Half Moon's summit). South Face has one author only (the same person wrote the South Face page, the North Ridge page and the peak page). The North Ridge has two independent accounts: that route page (2005/2008), and a 2013 trip report by a different climber. They agree on these points. The route starts at the deep notch north of the peak, reached by the scree gully that leaves the Kangaroo Pass path about 2 miles from the car. The route page says to look east for the prominent scree gully; the report ends with a slog through loose scree. The route page's approach note, credited to a third climber, says to cross the last soggy meadow before Kangaroo Pass and take the talus gully angling back to the notch north of Half Moon. The route is seven pitches; the report says belay at the obvious ledges for 7 pitches. The rock is eroded or friable low and much better higher. The line stays on or west of the crest: the route page puts pitch 6 west of the crest, and the report has pitch 6 traversing the right (west) side with big exposure over the west face. The last pitch is easy to the summit. The descent is by rappelling the route: the route page says double ropes and slings for rappels, and the report made four 40-50 m rappels. They differ on anchors: in 2005-08 the route page found no fixed gear or rappel anchors, while the 2013 party found pitons, a 1/4-inch bolt, a slung horn with a fixed nut and two new 3/8-inch bolts. The rappel text says anchors vary and may be absent. GRADE CAVEAT FOR THE OWNER: only the route page states a number (5.7+, Grade III). The 2013 report calls the route one of the few 'moderate' multi-pitch lines, and the peak entry puts the easiest route at fifth class. The number is written from the one numeric source, corroborated in kind but not in number. Pitch-level facts that only one account gives are left out: the chimney pitch, the piton on P2, the rappel lengths and the bolt sizes. The row's itinerary and approach_variants already described the ramp to the notch north of Half Moon, which is this route's start, so the approach needed only its ending rewritten. PINS: 'Kangaroo Pass' (48.50157,-120.62226) is removed under rule 1. It is about 0.95 km south of the line from the 2-mile fork to the notch north of the summit, and the North Ridge approach leaves the path before the pass. 'Class 4 Step below the Summit' (48.50738,-120.61612) is removed because it marks a feature of the non-existent scramble on the south-southwest side. It is about 340 m from the summit, so it falls under rule 3 rather than rule 1's 500 m test. 'Heather Gully Descent Cutoff' has no coordinates, so apply-pins cannot remove it by coordinate; it is dropped inside the waypoints `set` text op, and no other pin's lat/lng changes. The fork pin keeps its position (2 mi, which both accounts support) and gets a new name and note. The summit's distMi (4, from the old Kangaroo Pass route) is set null. NOT CHANGED, for the owner: dist_km 12.87 and gain_ft/loss_ft 3200 were built for the Kangaroo Pass line, and no source states this approach's one-way distance or gain. timing is set null because its 10.5 h was for the non-existent scramble. difficulty.technical=2 is a computed estimate that should be recomputed for 5.7+. The 'Early Winters Creek Clearing' pin sits about 450 m NORTH of the trailhead, while the path runs south; that is under 500 m, so it was left and flagged. No pin exists for the notch where the route starts; none could be placed from two sources.

ops.expect: Half Moon is a crescent-shaped granite fin on the north half of Kangaroo Ridge, between Wallaby Peak (0.23 mi south, the peak's higher neighbor) and Big Kangaroo (8,326 ft) to the north. It sits about two miles east of, and in clear view from, the North Cascades Highway at Washington Pass. The rock is ~45-million-year-old rapakivi-textured granite of the Golden Horn batholith. Fred and Helmy Beckey, with Walt Varney, made the first ascent on June 17, 1942. There is no easy walk-up: at least three technical lines are known (Southwest Ridge, North Ridge, South Face), all involving sustained Class 3-4 scrambling with at least one low-5th-class move. This route takes the Southwest Ridge, generally regarded as the least difficult option, which finishes with a short, low-exposure Class 4 step just below the summit.
ops.value: Half Moon is a crescent-shaped granite fin on the north half of Kangaroo Ridge, between Wallaby Peak and Big Kangaroo, about two miles east of the North Cascades Highway at Washington Pass. It has no easy way up: every line to its summit is a roped rock climb, and the easiest is fifth class. The North Ridge starts in the deep notch just north of the fin and climbs about seven pitches on or just west of the crest to the summit. The rock is friable and eroded on the first pitch or two and much better above, and the upper ridge has real exposure over the west face. Fred and Helmy Beckey and Walt Varney made the first ascent of the peak on June 17, 1942. The route sees few parties, so expect lichen, some loose rock and anchors that may need rebuilding.

ops.expect: Half Moon is a SW-to-NE trending rock fin on Kangaroo Ridge between Wallaby Peak and Big Kangaroo, with solid, steep, crack-laden faces. Documented lines include the 1942 first-ascent (original) route, rated roughly Class 5+ (low 5th class) — the easiest known way to the summit — plus at least one modern route, Uncle Wehrly's Toupee (5.10-, trad), and at least 3 other difficult unnamed technical lines. None of these is a non-technical scramble.
ops.value: Start in the deep notch north of the peak and climb the broad buttress above it toward the ridge crest. The first pitch has hollow, friable rock that improves steadily on the second. From there the line stays on the crest or just west of it, belaying at ledges, with steeper crack climbing in the middle of the route. High on the ridge a pitch traverses the west side of the narrowing crest with big exposure over the west face before working back to the crest. The last pitch is easy climbing on the crest, then a short scramble to the summit. Seven pitches is the usual count; belay at the obvious ledges rather than running pitches together, which causes rope drag.

ops.value: The route is descended by rappelling the line of ascent back to the notch. Carry two ropes. Anchors are a mix of fixed pitons, bolts, slung horns and nuts of varying age, and some parties have found none at all, so bring slings and cord to back up or build each station.

ops.expect: Reverse the Southwest Ridge. Most parties avoid down-climbing the full lower ridge crest by dropping west into the obvious heather gully toward Early Winters Creek partway down.
ops.value: Rappel the North Ridge back to the notch north of the peak, then descend the scree gully and reverse the approach to the highway.

ops.expect: Descend by reversing the ascent line rather than continuing over the ridge. From the summit, downclimb back to the flat belay ledge about 200 ft below the top; this is where the route's one unavoidable technical bit lives — an open-book crack beside a 60-degree slab (roughly a 60 ft 5.6 pitch on the way up). Most parties do not downclimb this: rappel from slung webbing around a large block on the southwest side of the peak just below the summit to get back down past this section. This is a natural gear/block anchor, not bolted — inspect any existing tat before trusting it and back it up if it looks tired. A single rappel here is on the order of 100-150 ft, so a 60 m rope (doubled) covers it comfortably, and a 30 m single-strand rappel is enough if you stop at the first good ledge/stance; parties differ on exactly where they break it depending on rope length carried, but one rappel is the norm to clear the crux. Below the rappel, continue down the loose class 2-3 southwest gully, taking care with scree and rockfall onto anyone below. Rather than downclimbing the full lower southwest ridge, most parties drop west off the crest partway down into the obvious heather gully, which avoids the worst of the loose rock in the lower gully. From there, cross back over the low notch/ridge point into the basin below Wallaby's south slopes, contour west back to Kangaroo Pass, and descend the climbers' path back through the boulder fields and across the avalanche path to the Hairpin Turn pullout.
ops.value: Descend the route. From the summit, downclimb the easy but exposed top of the ridge to the first anchor and rappel back down the line of ascent, using the ledges on the crest and its west side as stations, until you are back in the notch north of the peak. Carry two ropes; the stations are a mix of old fixed pitons, bolts, slung horns and nuts, some parties have found no fixed anchors at all, and any tat left there should be inspected and backed up. From the notch, descend the loose scree gully carefully (keep the party close to limit rockfall), and at its foot rejoin the climbers' path and follow it back north to the hairpin pullout on the highway.

ops.expect: Mostly unroped Class 3-4; a short rope and a few small cams/slings are useful for the exposed summit blocks.
ops.value: A medium alpine rack of nuts and cams protects the route; the cracks take gear well once past the eroded rock on the first pitch. Bring plenty of slings, and two ropes for the rappel descent.

ops.expect: Retreat is straightforward down the southwest slopes at almost any point.
ops.value: Retreat is by rappel down the line of ascent from almost any belay ledge, back to the notch north of the peak; carry enough slings and cord to leave anchors. Below the notch, the scree gully leads back to the climbers' path.

ops.expect: Park at the large Hairpin Turn pullout on Highway 20 near milepost 163 (roughly 5,100 ft), just east of Washington Pass — this doubles as the trailhead for Kangaroo Pass. From the east end of the pullout, drop into the woods and pick up the unsigned but well-used climbers' path (no official trail number; this is the standard Kangaroo Ridge/Wallaby/Half Moon approach). The path runs south, staying west of and well above Early Winters Creek — do not angle down toward the creek itself, a common route-finding mistake. Around 1 mile in you pass a small clearing near the creek where old small-plane wreckage is still visible, a useful landmark that you're on line. Beyond this the path climbs through boulder fields and slab benches with intermittent cairns (route-finding gets genuinely tricky here in fog or fresh snow — the tread all but disappears on the slabs), crossing the toe of the avalanche path that sheds off the col between South Early Winters Spire and Cornice Peak; this slope is a hazard in early-season or after fresh snow and should be crossed with care or avoided later in the day once it's baked in the sun. The path gains the ridge at Kangaroo Pass (~6,670 ft, about 1.5-2 miles and roughly an hour of hiking from the car). From the pass, contour east below Wallaby's south slopes, staying just below the crest, until you can cross over the ridge at a low notch north of Half Moon into the basin on its southwest side — this puts you at the base of the broad southwest gully/slopes that give the route its name. Water is only reliably available near Early Winters Creek in the first mile; carry what you need above the pass. From the base of the gully, the route climbs class 2-3 talus and loose scree — rockfall is a real concern with any party above you — before the gully narrows to a steeper class 4 step of cleaner rock roughly midway up; above that, scrambling leads to a flat belay ledge about 200 ft below the true summit, where the final short technical section begins.
ops.value: Park at the large hairpin-turn pullout on Highway 20 near milepost 163 (roughly 5,100 ft), just east of Washington Pass. From the east end of the pullout, drop into the woods and pick up the unsigned but well-used climbers' path toward Kangaroo Pass. It runs south, staying west of and well above Early Winters Creek — angling down toward the creek itself is the common route-finding mistake. Beyond the first mile the path climbs through boulder fields and slab benches with intermittent cairns, and the tread all but disappears on the slabs, so route-finding is tricky in fog or fresh snow. It also crosses the toe of the avalanche path that sheds off the col between South Early Winters Spire and Cornice Peak, a hazard in early season or after new snow. About two miles from the car, cross the last soggy meadow before the path climbs toward Kangaroo Pass and leave it: look up and left (east) for the prominent talus and scree gully that angles back to the deep notch just north of Half Moon. Climb it — a loose slog at the end — to the notch, where the route starts. Water is only reliably available near Early Winters Creek low on the approach; carry what you need above it.

expect.baseFinding: HALF MOON IS A FIN, AND THAT IS HOW YOU KNOW YOU ARE UNDER IT. It is a thin, crescent-shaped rock blade trending southwest to northeast, sitting between Wallaby Peak to the south and Big Kangaroo to the north; a broad blocky summit mass with a wide gully splitting it is Wallaby, not this. Aim for the notch immediately NORTH of the fin, gained by the talus ramp that angles back from the meadow below Kangaroo Pass, and cross there into the basin on the southwest side. The route begins at the foot of the broad gully draining that southwest flank. Climb loose class 2-3 talus and scree until the gully pinches down to a short step of noticeably cleaner, more solid rock about halfway up — that step is your confirmation you are in the right gully rather than a neighbouring one. Above it, scrambling reaches a flat belay ledge about 200 ft below the true summit, where the short technical finish starts.

expect.name: Three-Route Fork below Kangaroo Pass
expect.note: Boot path splits toward Half Moon's three route options here; stay on the Southwest Ridge line rather than continuing straight up to the Kangaroo Pass notch.
expect.directions: Above the clearing the path climbs through boulder fields and slab benches marked only by intermittent cairns, and the tread all but disappears on the slabs — this is the hardest stretch to follow in fog or fresh snow. It also crosses the toe of the avalanche path that sheds off the col between South Early Winters Spire and Cornice Peak, which is a hazard in early season or after new snow and is better crossed early than once the slope has baked in the sun.

expect.name: Kangaroo Pass
expect.note: Broad saddle on Kangaroo Ridge shared with approaches to Wallaby Peak and Big Kangaroo; gain the ridge here and traverse toward Half Moon's southwest side.

expect.name: Class 4 Step below the Summit
expect.note: A short, exposed Class 4 slab step breaks up the otherwise Class 3 Southwest Ridge just below the top; loose blocks reported, test holds before committing.
expect.directions: From the pass, contour east below Wallaby's south slopes, staying just under the crest, until you can cross back over the ridge at a low notch north of Half Moon into the basin on its southwest side. That drops you at the foot of the broad southwest gully, which starts as Class 2-3 talus and loose scree where rockfall from any party above you is the real danger. Higher up the gully narrows and steepens onto cleaner rock.

expect.name: Half Moon Summit
expect.note: Crescent-shaped granite high point of Kangaroo Ridge climbing, first ascended June 17, 1942 by Fred and Helmy Beckey with Walt Varney.

expect.name: Heather Gully Descent Cutoff
expect.note: Partway down the ridge, cut west off the rock into a steep heather-and-dirt gully dropping directly toward Early Winters Creek; loose footing and easy to lose the boot path in poor visibility.

value.name: SR-20 Hairpin / Pond Pullout (east of Washington Pass)
value.note: Large paved pullout on Highway 20 just east of Washington Pass, below Liberty Bell/South Early Winter Spire; pick up cairns leading south through brush toward Early Winters Creek.
value.directions: Take Highway 20 to the large hairpin-turn pullout near milepost 163, just east of Washington Pass, at roughly 5,100 ft. It is a big paved pullout sitting below Liberty Bell and South Early Winter Spire, and it doubles as the trailhead for Kangaroo Pass. Park here and start from the east end of the lot, where cairns lead south through the brush toward Early Winters Creek.

value.name: Early Winters Creek Clearing (Airplane Wreckage)
value.note: Small clearing along Early Winters Creek scattered with old wreckage from a small-plane crash; last reliable water before the boot path climbs away from the creek.
value.directions: Drop into the woods from the east end of the pullout and pick up the unsigned but well-used climbers' path. It runs south, staying west of and well above Early Winters Creek; angling down toward the creek itself is the standard route-finding mistake on this stretch. Reaching the clearing at about a mile confirms you are still on line.

results.resolution: delete_recommended (rule 3: no 'East Face' 5.6 climb exists on Liberty Bell; every documented Liberty Bell route already has its own row, and the beta the row carries belongs to Lexington Tower's East Face, which also has its own row, wa_lexington_tower_east_face)
results.summary: Delete this row: Liberty Bell has no easy East Face route, every real Liberty Bell climb already has its own row, and the row's actual beta belongs to Lexington Tower's East Face, which also has one.
results.evidence: Two independent route lists for Liberty Bell were checked. The Mountain Project area lists 19 routes; the summitpost peak page (archived) says the east face holds steep big-wall climbs, the south and west faces hold the modest 5.6-5.9 climbs, and the Beckey Route (5.6, southwest face) is the easiest of the peak's established routes. The encyclopedia list was also read but copies the Mountain Project set, so it is not counted as a separate source. Neither list has a route called East Face, and nothing on the east face is below 5.10: Freedom Rider 5.10d, Liberty Crack 5.11a / C2, Thin Red Line 5.12, Independence 5.12a, Live Free or Die, Liberty and Injustice, Freedom or Death, A Servant To Liberty, Dark Side of Liberty. All 19 listed routes have their own rows on wa_liberty_bell, matched name for name against the live sibling list, including the only 5.6 route (wa_liberty_bell_beckey_route, Grade II, 5.6, 4 pitches, SW face). The row's live beta ('ten pitches... slopey pitch 1 traverse... offwidth crux (pitch 6) passing a fixed 2x4 and two bolts to an alcove') is Lexington Tower's East Face, and its own corrections note admits the header facts were copied from there; that climb is wa_lexington_tower_east_face. The row's 4-pitch 5.4-5.6 pitch table and 'popular, lower-grade line' framing match no source, and they describe the Beckey Route's grade and length on the wrong face. There is no documented climb to rewrite the row as, so it should be deleted. No ops are written.
